new_statements.quote: Last but not least, lexical stress functions as a culminative, hierarchical, delimitative and rhythmic unit [9], falling regularly on the penultimate syllable. Typologically, Nahuatl has a polysynthetic structure with the possibility of the object and even some modifiers being incorporated to the verb root. Structures above five or six syllables are not the most frequent, but they are not unusual either. In such words secondary stress is found. According to Kager's classification [9], these synthetic structures in Morelos Nahuatl are typical of a bound or limited system, which is also non-sensitive to quantity, and it assigns stress from right to left, producing left-oriented, i.e. trochaic feet: [nik.ˌkʷah.kʷal.ˌt͡ɬaʃ.kal.ˈma.ka]
new_statements.citation: Velázquez Patiño, Eduardo Patricio. 2014. Intonation patterns of Morelos Nahuatl. In N. Campbell, D. Gibbon & D. Hirst (eds.), Proceedings of Speech Prosody 7 (Dublin), 487-491. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2014-85
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable; vowel length does not attract stress (quantity-insensitive). Whorf 1946 (Milpa Alta/Tepoztlán, snippet-reconstructed, p. 369) says the same: 'Words over one syllable have primary accent on the penult'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Velázquez Patiño: in long polysynthetic words (over 5-6 syllables) secondary stress is assigned right-to-left in binary trochaic feet, e.g. [nik.ˌkʷah.kʷal.ˌt͡ɬaʃ.kal.ˈma.ka]; primary vs secondary difference is only relative (p. 489). Whorf 1946 p. 370 (snippet): secondary accent on an ultima ending in -C and on the first syllable of a long word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for native words. Whorf 1946 p. 381 (snippet): final accent in Hispanized place names only, 'in Aztec they are accented on the penult'. Loanword stress not discussed by Velázquez Patiño.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress; data from read sentences and elicited spontaneous utterances of Cuentepec speakers (one young male for vowel study; 3 speakers for intonation); all three correlates (intensity, duration, F0) signal stress but F0 is the only constant one (p. 488); stress interacts with a phonemic vowel length contrast that is 'not robust' in Cuentepec.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes the Cuentepec (municipio Temixco) variety of Morelos Nahuatl, squarely within more1259 / ISO nhm. The secondary corroboration (Whorf 1946) describes Milpa Alta (Mexico City) with notes on Tepoztlán, Morelos; Glottolog files Whorf's sketch under more1259, but Milpa Alta itself is geographically outside Morelos. Tetelcingo Nahuatl (tete1251, nhg), also in Morelos, is a separate languoid and was not used.
